title: Will Aliens Arrive Soon? Harvard Professor Avi Loeb Strongly Debunks Viral Rumours
excerpt: Avi Loeb denies a viral 16-day alien prediction, explaining how the false claim differs from his documented $1,000 wager over a 2030 discovery.
content:
Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb denied predicting that aliens would reveal themselves within 16 days, rejecting a claim that circulated on social media in October 2026.

Speaking on NewsNation's Jesse Weber Live, the professor said the statement attributed to him was false and accused those spreading it of seeking attention.

The denial followed social media posts suggesting Loeb had forecast an imminent extraterrestrial revelation. Although the claim appeared on pop culture and sports-related accounts, its original source remains unclear.

Loeb's documented scientific wager concerns possible evidence of extraterrestrial intelligence by December 2030, not an alien arrival within days.

Avi Loeb Slams Viral Alien Prediction as 'Clickbait'

During his NewsNation appearance, Loeb said people could mistake the alleged prediction for a genuine scientific statement.

'Some people may believe it,' he warned. The Harvard professor accused people of attributing to him comments he never made. He suggested the misleading claim was intended to attract attention rather than accurately represent his research.

'It's obvious that there are people who want to get attention by ascribing things that I don't say. In this case, they wanted to get clickbait. They did get it.'

His remarks challenged the prediction's credibility, although the intentions of those sharing it have not been independently established.

In a separate statement reproduced from X, Loeb rejected the suggestion that the alleged countdown reflected his scientific position. 'The claim made in this post is false and does not accurately represent my views or scientific work.'

He also emphasised the importance of intellectual honesty and scientific rigour when investigating possible extraterrestrial technology.

The distinction matters because Loeb has openly supported examining unconventional astronomical possibilities. However, investigating a hypothesis is fundamentally different from confirming a discovery or predicting when extraterrestrial contact might occur.

Avi Loeb's $1,000 Alien Wager Has a December 2030 Deadline

Although Loeb rejected the 16-day prediction, he is involved in a documented wager concerning the possible discovery of extraterrestrial intelligence.

In 2025, American science historian Michael Shermer challenged Loeb over whether qualifying evidence of extraterrestrial visitation would receive scientific confirmation by 31 December 2030.

The $1,000 wager, registered through the Long Now Foundation's Long Bets programme, lists Shermer as the predictor and Loeb as the challenger.

Shermer argues that the specified discovery or disclosure will not happen before the deadline. Loeb accepted the opposing position, reflecting his optimism about finding evidence of extraterrestrial technology.

Importantly, the wager establishes specific conditions for determining whether such a discovery has occurred.

Under its terms, at least two of three organisations must affirm that the evidence qualifies. Those organisations are NASA, the National Science Foundation and the American Astronomical Society.

The discovery must involve extraterrestrial intelligence demonstrated through technological objects, including qualifying UAPs, UFOs or interstellar objects. The terms also allow for the discovery of an alien biological life form on Earth.

Regardless of the outcome, the $1,000 stake will go to the Galileo Project Foundation. The wager does not require aliens to appear publicly, announce their existence or arrive on a predetermined date.

Why Avi Loeb's Alien Research Continues To Draw Attention

Loeb's involvement in the wager reflects his broader interest in searching for extraterrestrial technology. He heads the Galileo Project, which investigates unidentified anomalous phenomena and interstellar objects through scientific observations.

In 2025, Loeb attracted attention after suggesting that the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS might have an artificial extraterrestrial origin. That possibility remained speculative, not an established scientific finding.

NASA identifies 3I/ATLAS as an interstellar comet, first reported on 1 July 2025. The agency says its characteristics, including an icy nucleus and surrounding gas and dust, are consistent with natural cometary activity.

The distinction between unexplained observations and evidence of alien technology also extends to government investigations.

In its 2024 historical review, the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office reported finding no verified evidence that investigated UAP sightings represented extraterrestrial technology.

For the documented 2030 wager to favour Loeb, at least two specified scientific organisations would need to confirm qualifying evidence before the deadline. Nothing in those conditions establishes a date for extraterrestrial visitors to appear. The supposed 16-day prediction remains a claim Loeb says he never made.
